segments.translit:
kukkurīpādena bho yogin aṅgulim ūrddhīkṛtyokta[ḥ] etat trailokyām iti kāyavākcittasyābhāsadoṣo mahāsukhena jitaḥ |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ —
ghara acchante mā jāṅga vaṇetyādi | 48 ||
segments.translation: O [yogi]{yogi}, [Kukkurīpāda]{p-kukkuri}, raising his [finger]{anguli} upward, has said: 'these [three worlds]{trailokya}', that is, the fault of [appearance]{abhasa} of [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta} is conquered by [great bliss]{mahasukha}. And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says: 'While there is a home, do not go to the forest', and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the last couplet as Kukkurīpāda, finger raised, addressing the yogi; 'these [three worlds]{trailokya}' (literally 'this threefold world') he glosses as great bliss conquering the fault of appearance of body, speech and mind. He gives the gesture no reading. His words make the world what is conquered; the Tibetan line 5b makes 'this' the conqueror (cp.48.m1).

equations.en: body, speech and mind, whose fault of appearance is conquered by great bliss

citations.quoted: ghara acchante mā jāṅga vaṇe… (While there is a home, do not go to the forest…)
citations.work: a verse of Saraha (Sarahapāda); Munidatta does not name the work, and the Tibetan has it as khyim ni yod bzhin nags su 'gro bar ma byed cig

flags.note: Munidatta cites 'etat trailokyam' ('this threefold world'; the manuscript writes trailokyām) and glosses it with a passive, 'is conquered (jitaḥ) by great bliss': in his text the three worlds are what is conquered. The Tibetan line 5b, ''di ni 'jig rten gsum du bde ba chen pos rgyal', makes 'this' the conqueror ('This conquers the three worlds by great bliss', as drafted), and the Tibetan comment follows its own line ('dis, 'by this'; skyon las … rgyal, 'is victorious over the fault'). The Old Bengali line Munidatta read may have had 'this threefold world' as subject of a passive; that cannot be checked. Not harmonized: the comment is translated as the Sanskrit stands, and the draft line as the Tibetan stands.

The Sanskrit is a fragment of the comment on couplet 5 only. The Tibetan parallel opens with words it lacks: 'rkang pa bzhi pas 'bras bu'i ngo bo gsungs te / gyen du zhes bya ba la sogs pa', 'With the fourth verse he states the nature of the fruit: "upward" and so on'. The rest of Munidatta's Sanskrit on song 48 is lost with the song; cp.48.m2–m6 are the Tibetan translators' comment.

aṅgulimūrddhīkṛtya: read aṅgulim ūrdhvīkṛtya, 'raising the finger upward' (ūrddhī is the Bengali-script spelling of ūrdhvī). The Tibetan comment's 'sor mo'i steng du byas pa', 'made on top of the finger', renders the words one by one; the Tibetan line 5a has 'sor mo gyen du bslang nas', 'raising the finger upward'. Munidatta repeats the gesture and gives it no reading.

ukta[ḥ]: the visarga is Shastri's restoration. Read uktaḥ, the sentence could also be construed '[you], O yogi, are told by Kukkurīpāda'; uktam would be 'it is said'. The sense is the same either way; I rendered 'has said'.

Saraha's line 'ghara acchante mā jāṅga vaṇe': jāṅga is unclear, apparently a form of 'go' (compare Apabhraṃśa jāhu), which the Tibetan ''gro bar ma byed cig', 'do not go', supports. ghara acchante could also mean 'while staying at home'; I followed the Tibetan 'khyim ni yod bzhin', 'while there is a home'. The closing ৪৮ (48) marks the end of the comment on song 48 and is not translated.

segments.translit: /de kho na nyid kyi don sgra gzhan gyis kuk+ku rI pa'i zhabs kyis gsungs te/
segments.translation: [Kukkurīpāda]{p-kukkuri} states the meaning of [reality]{tattva} in other words:
segments.note: Munidatta's Sanskrit is lost; the Tibetan translators' comment, a translation of his we cannot check, opens: Kukkurīpāda states the meaning of [reality]{tattva} in other words. 'The meaning of reality' (de kho na nyid kyi don) may render a Sanskrit 'that same meaning' (tam evārtham?), which would make this Munidatta's usual way of introducing a song (cp.48.m2).

flags.note: Survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), standing in for Munidatta's lost Sanskrit; translated from the Tibetan.

de kho na nyid kyi don is rendered as it stands, 'the meaning of reality' (de kho na nyid regularly translates tattva). With sgra gzhan gyis, 'in other words', it may instead render tam evārtham, 'that same meaning', the formula by which Munidatta links a song to what precedes it (compare his opening of song 12, cp.12.m1, as the glossary reports it; and don de nyid, 'that same meaning', in cp.48.m5). Then: 'Kukkurīpāda states that same meaning in other words.' Without the Sanskrit this cannot be settled.

segments.translit: rdo rje zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni yul gyi sgra'i g.yul ngo 'gog pa'i phyir rdo rje dang chu skyes de bzhin du thabs dang shes rab bde ba chen po'i rang bzhin kuk+ku rI'i zhabs kyis 'dren par byed do/ /mnyam nyid ces pa ni rang bzhin gcig tu bde ba chen po'i ngo bo nyid rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug gi mnyam pa nyid du sbyor ba de nyid de'i dA ri kA'o/ /de bzhin du lung las kyang / dngos po gcig gi de nyid gang gis mthong / /dngos kun de nyid nges mthong ngo bo gcig /dngos po kun gyi ngo bo rang bzhin rnams/ /dngos kun gcig gi rang bzhin ngo bo nyid/
segments.translation: '[Vajra]{vajra}' and so on: to stop the [battle]{battle}front of the sound of [sense objects]{visaya}, [Kukkurīpāda]{p-kukkuri} leads the [vajra]{vajra} and the [lotus]{lotus}, and likewise [means]{upaya} and [wisdom]{prajna}, whose [nature]{svabhava} is [great bliss]{mahasukha}. '[Sameness]{samata}' means: that very [union]{mela} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} in [sameness]{samata} with the essence of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, as one [nature]{svabhava}, is its dārikā. Likewise [scripture]{agama} too says: 'Whoever sees the [reality]{tattva} of one thing / surely sees the [reality]{tattva} of all things: their essence is one. / The essences, the [nature]{svabhava}s, of all things: / all things have the [nature]{svabhava} and essence of one.'
segments.note: Munidatta's Sanskrit is lost; the Tibetan translators' comment, a translation of his we cannot check, sets vajra and lotus beside means and wisdom, led to stop 'the battlefront of the sound of sense objects' (obscure); sameness is the lord of yogis' union with [great bliss]{mahasukha} as one nature. The gloss ends in an untranslated transcription, dā ri kā (cp.48.m3).

equations.en: the union of the lord of yogis in sameness with the essence of great bliss, as one nature

citations.quoted: dngos po gcig gi de nyid gang gis mthong / dngos kun de nyid nges mthong ngo bo gcig / dngos po kun gyi ngo bo rang bzhin rnams / dngos kun gcig gi rang bzhin ngo bo nyid
citations.work: an unnamed scripture (lung, presumably Sanskrit āgama); perhaps the verse eko bhāvaḥ sarvabhāvasvabhāvaḥ … that Madhyamaka authors quote (identified from memory, unchecked)

flags.note: Survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), standing in for Munidatta's lost Sanskrit; translated from the Tibetan.

yul gyi sgra'i g.yul ngo, 'the battlefront of the sound of sense objects', is obscure. sgra may stand for śabda in the sense 'word' ('the battlefront that the word "objects" names'?), or sound may be meant as one of the objects; the Sanskrit is lost. Rendered literally. The glossary's battle entry already records this phrase as obscure.

Vajra and lotus are set beside means and wisdom with de bzhin du, 'likewise', not equated with them by an explicit gloss, so no equation is recorded. 'whose nature is great bliss' (bde ba chen po'i rang bzhin) may qualify means and wisdom or all four. 'dren par byed, 'leads', suits the army of the song; it can also mean 'brings in, introduces', as of an image or a quotation.

de nyid de'i dA ri kA'o, 'that very thing is its dārikā': dA ri kA is a transcription the translators left untranslated, and nothing in the comment explains it. Possibilities include Sanskrit dārikā, 'girl' (compare the dārī of song 28, which the glossary records Munidatta glossing as dārikā, cp.28.m5), the name Dārika (Tibetan dA ri ka), or a word of the lost Old Bengali line that the comment cited. None is evident, so the word is left as it stands.

The gloss on sameness is loosely built: rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug gi mnyam pa nyid du sbyor ba may be 'the lord of yogis' union in sameness' (taken here) or 'the joining [of great bliss] in the sameness of the lord of yogis'. rang bzhin gcig tu, 'as one nature', may go with either.

The last two lines of the scripture verse are elliptic (dngos po kun gyi ngo bo rang bzhin rnams / dngos kun gcig gi rang bzhin ngo bo nyid); the sense seems to be that one thing is the nature of all things and all things the nature of one. Rendered closely. dngos po is rendered 'thing' and left unmarked: the glossary's entry for dngos po (bhava-being) has 'being', which does not suit 'one thing … all things'.

segments.translit: /d+h+rU'i rkang pas bde ba chen po'i mthu gsungs te/ bcom zhes pa ni bde ba chen po zhes pa thos pa tsam gyis srid pa'i dkyil 'khor gyi yul dang dbang po 'di dag bcom pa'o/
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he states the [power]{prabhava} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}. 'Destroyed' means: merely by hearing the words '[great bliss]{mahasukha}', these [sense objects]{visaya} and [senses]{indriya} of the [maṇḍala]{mandala} of [existence]{bhava} are destroyed.
segments.note: Munidatta's Sanskrit is lost; the Tibetan translators' comment, a translation of his we cannot check, says the refrain states the [power]{prabhava} of great bliss: 'destroyed' means that merely hearing the words 'great bliss' destroys these sense objects and senses of the maṇḍala of existence. It does not take up 2b, emptiness the king (cp.48.m4).

equations.en: these sense objects and senses of the maṇḍala of existence, destroyed merely by hearing the words 'great bliss'

flags.note: Survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), standing in for Munidatta's lost Sanskrit; translated from the Tibetan.
srid pa'i dkyil 'khor gyi yul dang dbang po 'di dag: I took 'of the maṇḍala of existence' with both the sense objects and the senses; it could go with the objects alone.
The comment explains only bcom, 'destroyed' (2a). Whether 'merely hearing the words "great bliss"' looks to 2b, where emptiness, the king, is named great bliss, it does not say.

segments.translit: /rkang pa gnyis pas don de nyid gsal bar mdzad do/ /sgrogs pa zhes bya ba la sogs pa'i gzhom du med pa'i dbyangs zhes pa ni rnga sgra dang dung sgra g.yul ngor sgrogs te/ gang stong pa nyid kyi dbus su bskyed pas kye'i rnal 'byor pas srid pa'i g.yul gyi dpung rang bzhin med par gyis shig pa'o/
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he makes that same meaning clear. In 'proclaimed' and so on, 'the [unstruck]{anahata} melodies' means: the sound of the [drum]{drum} and the sound of the [conch]{conch} proclaim at the [battle]{battle}front. Since they are produced in the midst of [emptiness]{sunyata}, O [yogi]{yogi}, make the [army]{army} of the [battle]{battle} of [existence]{bhava} [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}!
segments.note: Munidatta's Sanskrit is lost; the Tibetan translators' comment, a translation of his we cannot check, says this verse clarifies the same point: the [unstruck]{anahata} melodies are the drum and conch sounds proclaimed at the battlefront, produced in the midst of [emptiness]{sunyata}; and it tells the yogi to make the army of the battle of existence without intrinsic nature (cp.48.m5).

equations.en: the sound of the drum and the sound of the conch proclaimed at the battlefront, produced in the midst of emptiness

flags.note: Survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), standing in for Munidatta's lost Sanskrit; translated from the Tibetan. 'The second verse' is couplet 3, by Munidatta's count, which leaves out the refrain.

gang stong pa nyid kyi dbus su bskyed pas: I took gang, 'which', as the drum and conch sounds, produced in the midst of emptiness. It could also mean 'by producing them in the midst of emptiness', making the yogi the one who produces them. kye'i rnal 'byor pas, with an odd genitive and an agentive ending, is read as a vocative, 'O yogi', with the imperative gyis shig.
The comment has dung sgra, 'the sound of the conch', where the line has dung skad, 'the call of the conch'; rendered as each stands.

segments.translit: /rkang pa gsum pas don dam pa byang chub kyi sems kyi rjes su bsngags pa gsungs te/ gsum zhes pa la sogs pa'i gsum ni bde ba chen po'i mes lus la sogs pa dkyil 'khor gsum gyi nyes pa bsregs nas bde ba chen po'i 'khor lo'i rtse mor gnas pas mi ltung ba'i bde ba chen po'i byang chub kyi sems kyi mes sdud par byed pa'o/ /de bzhin du ra ti badzra gyis kyang / byang chub sems ni spang mi bya/ /rdo rje pad+mas rgyas 'dabs pas/ /zhes so/
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks in [praise]{anusamsa} of [ultimate]{paramartha} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}. In 'three' and so on, 'three' means: having burnt with the [fire]{fire} of [great bliss]{mahasukha} the faults of the three [maṇḍala]{mandala}s, [body]{body} and the rest, and dwelling on the summit of the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}, he gathers in with the [fire]{fire} of the unfalling [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}. Likewise the [Rativajra]{tx-rativajra} too says: '[Bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} is not to be given up, / since [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus} seal it.'
segments.note: Munidatta's Sanskrit is lost; the Tibetan translators' comment, a translation of his we cannot check, calls this verse praise of ultimate [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}: the fire of great bliss burns the faults of the three maṇḍalas, 'body and the rest'; the town's summit is the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}'s summit, where one gathers with unfalling bodhicitta's fire (cp.48.m6).

equations.en: the three maṇḍalas, body and the rest

citations.quoted: byang chub sems ni spang mi bya / rdo rje pad+mas rgyas 'dabs pas

flags.note: Survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), standing in for Munidatta's lost Sanskrit; translated from the Tibetan. 'The third verse' is couplet 4, by Munidatta's count.

The comment makes fire the instrument ('with the fire of great bliss', mes) and names no agent; I supplied 'he'. The draft of 4a makes Fire the subject of both lines; the Tibetan line (me yis bsreg par byas) also allows '[he] burnt with fire'. Not harmonized: see questions.

Where the line has the summit of the town of bliss (bde ba'i grong khyer rtse mo), the comment puts the summit of the wheel of great bliss (bde ba chen po'i 'khor lo'i rtse mo): a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss. Fire is named a second time for the gathering of 4b (mes sdud par byed); what is gathered is not said (the line has thams cad, 'everything').
The three maṇḍalas are named only as 'body and the rest' (lus la sogs pa); body, speech and mind are presumably meant, but the comment does not list them.
In the Rativajra verse, rgyas 'dabs pas is probably for rgyas 'debs pas, 'because [it] seals'; rdo rje pad+mas may be 'by vajra and lotus' or 'by the vajra-lotus'.

questions: Line 5b: Munidatta's surviving Sanskrit (cp.48.m1) cites 'etat trailokyam', 'this threefold world', as what great bliss conquers; the draft follows the Tibetan line, 'This conquers the three worlds by great bliss', where 'this' is the conqueror. Should 5b carry a witness flag or note reporting Munidatta's reading?

Line 4a: the draft makes Fire the subject ('Fire burnt away … and, dwelling on the summit …, gathered everything in'). The Tibetan comment (cp.48.m6) takes fire as the instrument of an unnamed agent, who burns with the fire of great bliss and then, dwelling on the summit, gathers. The Tibetan line's me yis also allows 'with fire'. Reconsider the draft's subject?

cp.48.m2: I rendered de kho na nyid kyi don as it stands, 'the meaning of reality'. If you prefer the likely Sanskrit behind it (tam evārtham, 'that same meaning'), the sentence becomes 'Kukkurīpāda states that same meaning in other words.' Which do you want on the page?
cp.48.m3: dA ri kA is left untranslated as 'dārikā'. Is there a reading you know that should replace it, or should the transcription stand with the flag?

visaya: the draft's line 2a uses the surface 'objects' for {visaya}, but the glossary's approved English is 'sense objects', which I used in cp.48.m3 and m4. Add 'objects' as a listed variant, or change the draft?

trailokya: Munidatta's singular 'etat trailokyam' ('this threefold world') appears as 'these three worlds', to keep the approved English 'three worlds'. Acceptable, or should 'threefold world' become a variant?

cp.48.m3: the Tibetan has 'means and wisdom' (thabs dang shes rab) in that order, matching vajra and lotus. To keep the order I marked them separately as [means]{upaya} and [wisdom]{prajna}, not as the approved pair 'wisdom and means' {prajnopaya}. Is that right?

cp.48.m3: the scripture verse may be the Sanskrit 'eko bhāvaḥ sarvabhāvasvabhāvaḥ …', which Madhyamaka authors quote. I am working from memory and have not checked it. Can you confirm the source, or should the citation stay unnamed?
